    Evergreen Notes

    🌳 Evergreen planted Nov 9, 2023 tended Apr 12, 2026
    #evergreen#pkm#writing

    An evergreen note is written to be developed over time and across contexts rather than to be finished once. The term comes from Andy Matuschak. It is the single most useful idea I've adopted for thinking, and it's the load-bearing concept behind this whole On Tending a Digital Garden.

    The four properties #

    A good evergreen note is:

    1. Atomic — about exactly one idea. Atomicity is what makes a note linkable. You can't usefully link to "my thoughts on systems"; you can link to Idempotency Is a Superpower.
    2. Concept-oriented — titled as a claim or a concept, not a source or a date. The title is the API of the note.
    3. Densely linked — a note with no links is a leaf that will never be found again.
    4. Written in your own words — if you can't restate it, you don't have it yet.

    Atomicity, concretely #

    Compare two notes:

    ❌ "Notes on the time I broke production with a duplicate webhook"

    ✅ Idempotency Is a Superpower

    The first is a story; it's filed under one event and forgotten. The second is a concept I can link to from a stoicism note, a database note, or a gardening note. The story becomes evidence inside the concept note instead of being the note.

    How this differs from highlighting #

    Highlighting a book feels productive and teaches you nothing. The work is the re-expression. This is the whole argument of Book — How to Take Smart Notes, and it's why my book notes are short: the value isn't the quotes, it's the evergreen notes the quotes provoked.
